Here's how the game works and why commercial space can stay vacant:

This is very counter intuitive but a commercial investor isn't concerned with monthly cashflow, he is concerned with the peak income his property can earn in the year prior to the building being sold. This is because he isn't thinking about paying his monthly bills like a typical landlord, the commercial guy is going to the BIG BUCKS. He doesn't care if a commercial property loses money for a few years, he wants to resell the building for millions in profit. And you make the big money by having the property income "peak" a year or two before reselling it.

In the commercial world by focusing on the "peak income" it allows the property to be resold at a peak price (which can be sold without paying taxes, more on that later). This is oversimplifying but a commercial property is valued based on a "cap rate". You take the net income and divide it by the market cap rate and you arrive at the valuation of the property. So a cap rate of 5 would mean a property is selling for 20x its income (20=100/5). So if a property is being resold for 20x its net income you can see why landlords are looking for the high paying tenants and don't mind the property sitting vacant waiting on them

---Example time with math---

By way of example: Say in Manhattan the cap rate is 5%, and you own a building which earns $1,000,000 net revenue in a year. This building will be valued at $20,000,000 if it were sold to a real estate investment trust. The problem with holding the property is that the net revenue is taxed so it's not really that appealing to hold an asset for a few decades while taxes eat your profits alive. A more efficient tactic would be to focus all your energy on getting the revenue to $1,500,000 even if it means that your income in the earlier years suffers. As soon as you get the right leases in place you can resell the property for $30 million instead of $20,000,000. Assume a 10 year plan:

Scenario 1: $1,000,000 net revenue per year = $10,000,000 net revenue = $6,000,000 net revenue after taxes + $20,000,000 asset. During this time period the property was fully occupied and not an eye sore.

Scenario 2: $0 net revenue per year for first eight years while waiting for the "Big tenants". $1,500,000 net revenue in years 9 and 10 before the property is sold = $3,000,000 net revenue = $1,800,000 net revenue after taxes + $30,000,000 asset. For eight years the property was an eye sore while the company positioned the property for resale at peak revenue.

In both cases the company makes money, but in scenario 1 the company is eaten alive by taxes and has a $20,000,000 asset to show for it. In scenario 2 the company avoids taxes while the property is under performing until year 9&10 when it hits peak income. As a result in the later scenario the company is left with a $30,000,000 asset whose gains can be tax deferred and thus makes close to $10,000,000 more money while contributing nothing to the tax base.

Scenario 2 where a property has business vacancies for nearly a decade is terrible for the community at large, however it is brilliant in terms of making money for the property owner. Now it's way more complicated than this but never think a property owner is being stupid for leaving a store front vacant. You don't know the game like they do.
